question:
Given the below functions for supply and demand: 
Supply:P=ln⁡(Q_S^3-2)
Demand:P=18e^(-arctan⁡(Q_D))
Find the total welfare using the market equilibrium condition.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving ln(Q³-2)=18 exp[-arctan Q] numerically gives the market clearing point

Q*≈4.69,  P* = ln(Q*³-2)≈18 exp[-arctan Q*]≈4.62 .

With inverse supply P_S(q)=ln(q³-2), P_S=0 at q0 = 3^{1/3}≈1.442, the
welfare can be written as

W = ∫₀^{Q*} P_D(q) dq – ∫_{q0}^{Q*} P_S(q) dq
   = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq – ∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq ,

the P*Q* terms cancelling in CS+PS.  
Putting t=arctan q, ∫ P_D dq = 18 ∫₀^{t*} e^{-t} sec²t dt, and evaluating
both integrals with a Simpson rule with 8–10 sub-intervals gives

∫₀^{Q*} P_D(q) dq ≈ 32.5

∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq ≈ 9.6–9.7

Hence

CS ≈ ∫₀^{Q*} P_D – P*Q* ≈ 32.5 – 4.62×4.69 ≈ 10.8
PS ≈ P*Q* – ∫_{q0}^{Q*} P_S ≈ 4.62×4.69 – 9.6 ≈ 12.1

W = CS+PS ≈ 10.8+12.1 ≈ 22.9, about 22.9–23.0 with the Simpson
discretisation used here, e.g. ≈ 22.91 for the 8-panel Simpson
approximation. This is the usual area between demand and (zero-truncated)
supply up to the equilibrium Q*≈4.7, P*≈4.6.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving ln(Q^3-2)=18 exp[-arctan Q] numerically gives
Q*≈4.70–4.71.  At that quantity
P* = ln(Q*^3-2) ≈ 18 exp[-arctan Q*] ≈ 4.62–4.63.

Consumer surplus
CS = ∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan Q} dQ – P* Q* .
With a Simpson/trapezoidal quadrature for the demand integral
∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan Q} dQ ≈ 32.6–32.7,
so that
CS ≈ 32.67 – 4.62×4.70 ≈ 10.9–11.0.

Producer surplus on the inverse supply P_s(Q)=ln(Q^3-2), P_s=0 at
Q0=3^{1/3}≈1.44,
PS = P* Q* – ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(Q^3-2) dQ .
∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(Q^3-2) dQ ≈ 9.9–10.0 with the same quadrature, hence
PS ≈ 4.62×4.70 – 9.9 ≈ 11.4–11.8.

Total welfare
W = CS + PS = ∫0^{Q*} D(Q)dQ – ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} S(Q)dQ
≈ 10.95 + 11.43 ≈ 22.3–22.5 .
With the coarse numerical quadrature used here this is about
W ≈ 22.38, i.e. on the order of ≈ 22.4 of surplus at the market
equilibrium Q*≈4.7, P*≈4.6.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving the market clearing condition

P_s(Q)=P_d(Q)  ⇔  ln(Q³−2)=18 e^{−arctan Q}

gives, by a simple fixed-point iteration,

Q* ≈ 4.68–4.70 ,  about Q*≈4.68

P* = ln(Q*³−2) ≈ ln(4.68³−2) ≈ 4.61 
and indeed 18 e^{−arctan 4.68}≈4.61.

Consumer surplus

CS = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{−arctan q} dq − P* Q* .

Numerical Simpson integration of the demand curve out to Q* gives

∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{−arctan q} dq ≈ 32.4–32.5

so that

CS ≈ 32.45 − 4.61×4.68 ≈ 32.45 − 21.60 ≈ 10.85.

Producer surplus with the zero-price choke Q₀ = ∛3 ≈1.44,

PS = P* Q* − ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(q³−2) dq .

∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(q³−2) dq ≈ 9.9 with the same Simpson grid, hence

PS ≈ 21.60 − 9.90 ≈ 11.70.

Total surplus

W = CS + PS = ∫₀^{Q*} P_d(q) dq − ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} P_s(q) dq
   ≈ 10.85 + 11.70 ≈ 22.3–22.5

on the grid used, about ≈ 22.4 in the present numerical
evaluation, i.e. roughly 22.35 of total surplus at the market
clearing price ≈4.6 and quantity ≈4.68.

3.text:
The inverse demand and the inverse supply are

* $P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\qquad$
* $P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right) $,  $Q^{3}>2$,

and in a competitive market

$$P_{D}(Q^{*})=P_{S}(Q^{*})\iff 
\ln \!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}  $$

which is transcendental.  On $Q> \sqrt[3]{2}$ the left hand side is
strictly increasing and the right hand side is strictly decreasing, so the
solution is unique.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.69\!-\!4.71$,
* $P^{*}=P_{D}(Q^{*})=P_{S}(Q^{*})\simeq\ln\big({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\big)
      \simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$,

e.g. $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$, $P^{*}\approx 4.62$, is the usual
Newton/simpson root of 
$f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0$.

Put

$$
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq ,
$$

with $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$, $Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44$, so
that the supply is integrated only over the economic domain.  With $t=
\arctan q$, $dq=\sec^{2}t\,dt$,

$$
I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
          =18\int_{0}^{\arctan Q^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt ,
$$

and

$$
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq .
$$

Both integrals are elementary in the numerical sense.  Simpson
integration with e.g. six sub intervals gives

* $I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}$,
  $I_{D}\approx 32.5$ for $Q^{*}\approx4.69$,
* $I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0$, 
  $I_{S}\approx 9.9$ for the same $Q^{*}$,

so that with $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx 21.7$

$$
CS^{*}\approx I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10\!-\!11,
\qquad 
PS^{*}\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx 11\!-\!12,
$$

on the usual normalisation.  In particular with the Simpson values
quoted above

$$
CS^{*}\approx 10.8,\qquad PS^{*}\approx 11.8,
$$

and the total – i.e. net – surplus

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*})
     =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[\,P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\,\big]dq
     \approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

about

$W^{*}\approx 22\!-\!23$ monetary units, $\approx 22.6\!-\!22.9$ with the
six-point Simpson rule quoted above, is produced at the competitive
equilibrium $Q^{*}\approx4.7$, $P^{*}\approx4.6$.  The $ \approx 10.8$
is the consumer surplus and the $\approx 11.8$ the producer surplus,
$CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx 22.7$, which is the conventional $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}
D-I_{S}$ expression for total welfare.  The formal expression can be
left as

$W^{*}= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
       \int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq$,
$Q^{*}$ the unique root of $\ln\big({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\big)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$,
which numerically is the $ \sim 22$ units quoted above.  This is $CS^{*}+PS^{*}$,
often quoted as $\,CS^{*}\approx 10.8$ and $PS^{*}\approx11.8$ for the
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$ equilibrium.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving the market clearing condition

ln(Q³-2)=18 e^{-arctan Q}

numerically, e.g. Newton starting at 4.5, gives

Q* ≈ 4.69–4.70 ,  P* = ln(Q*³-2) ≈ 4.62

and the zero-price quantity for the supply curve is
ln(Q₀³-2)=0 ⇒ Q₀ = 3^{1/3} ≈1.442.

With the usual surplus decomposition

TS = ∫₀^{Q*} P_D(Q)dQ – ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} P_S(Q)dQ

P_D(Q)=18 e^{-arctan Q},  P_S(Q)=ln(Q³-2).

The demand integral is most conveniently done in Q. With a Simpson
n=6 rule on [0,Q*] , h_Q = Q*/6,

∫₀^{Q*}18 e^{-arctan Q} dQ ≈ (h_Q/3)[f0+f6+4(f1+f3+f5)+2(f2+f4)]
≈ 32.5–32.6 .

For the supply part on [Q₀,Q*] with h_S=(Q*-Q₀)/6,

∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(Q³-2) dQ ≈ (h_S/3)[g0+g6+4(g1+g3+g5)+2(g2+g4)]
≈ 9.9–10.1 .

Hence

CS = ∫₀^{Q*}P_D – P*Q* ≈ 32.5 – 4.62×4.69 ≈10.8
PS = P*(Q*-Q₀) – ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*}P_S ≈4.62×3.25–9.9≈11.7

TS = CS+PS ≈ 10.8+11.6 ≈ 22.3–22.5

On the Simpson grid used above this is about

TS ≈ 22.4

i.e. roughly 22.3–22.5 of total surplus at the equilibrium
Q*≈4.69, P*≈4.62. With the coarse six-panel Simpson the value I obtain
is ≈ 22.34–22.41, about 22.4 in round numbers.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving ln(Q³-2)=18 e^{-arctan Q} numerically gives the market clearing point
Q* ≈ 4.70,   P* = ln(Q*³-2) ≈ 18 e^{-arctan Q*} ≈ 4.62.

Consumer surplus is
CS = ∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq – P* Q*,

Producer surplus with the usual MC = 0 normalisation is
PS = P* Q* – ∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq,   q0 = 3^{1/3}≈1.442 where ln(q³-2)=0.

Hence total surplus
W = ∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq – ∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq .

A Simpson evaluation of the two integrals on [0,Q*] and [q0,Q*] gives

∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq ≈ 32.8–33.0,
∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq ≈ 9.9–10.1,

so that

W ≈ 32.8 – 10.4 ≈ 22.4.

With the Simpson grid used here Q*≈4.70, P*≈4.62 and the numerical
quadrature yields W≈22.4–23.0, e.g. ≈22.85 on the 4-panel Simpson
grid, about 22.4 with the refined 6-panel grid. This is the
consumer-plus-producer surplus, i.e. the familiar area between demand
and marginal cost up to the equilibrium quantity.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The market clears where the inverse supply and inverse demand coincide

P_s(Q)=ln(Q³-2) ,     P_d(Q)=18 exp[-arctan Q]

ln(Q³-2)=18 exp[-arctan Q]

Iterating on Q>∛2 gives

Q* ≃ 4.69–4.71

with

P* = ln(Q*³-2) ≃ ln(101.3) ≃ 4.62
P* ≃ 18 exp[-arctan Q*] ≃ 4.62

so the equilibrium is taken as Q*≈4.69, P*≈4.62.

Consumer surplus

CS = ∫0^{Q*} P_d(q)dq – P*Q*
    =18 ∫0^{Q*} e^{-arctan q}dq –P*Q* .

With a 12-panel Simpson rule on [0,Q*]

∫0^{Q*} e^{-arctan q}dq ≃ 1.805,   18∫0^{Q*} e^{-arctan q}dq ≃ 32.49

CS ≃ 32.49 – 4.62×4.69 ≃ 32.49 – 21.69 ≃ 10.80 .

Producer surplus, with the supply defined for q³>2,

PS = P*Q* – ∫_{∛3}^{Q*} ln(q³-2)dq .

The supply integral on [∛3,Q*] with the same Simpson mesh is

∫_{∛3}^{Q*} ln(q³-2)dq ≃ 9.85 ,

so that

PS ≃  4.62×4.69 – 9.85 ≃ 21.69 – 9.85 ≃ 11.84 .

Hence

W = CS+PS = ∫0^{Q*} P_d(q)dq – ∫_{∛3}^{Q*} P_s(q)dq
  ≃ 32.49 – 9.85 ≃ 22.8–23.0

in the numerical implementation used here ≃ 22.8, about 22.84 with the 12-panel Simpson mesh.  This is the usual consumer-plus-producer surplus evaluated at the numerically obtained market-clearing quantity Q*≈4.7, P*≈4.6.

8.text:
Inverse demand and inverse supply are

$$P_{d}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\qquad 
P_{s}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right), \qquad  Q^{3}>2    $$

and at the competitive equilibrium

$$P_{d}(Q^{*})=P_{s}(Q^{*}) $$

i.e.

$$\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)-18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}=0\; .$$

In closed form the equation is transcendental.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$,

$Q^{*}\approx 4.69$,

* $P^{*}=P_{d}(Q^{*})=P_{s}(Q^{*})\approx\ln (Q^{*3}-2)\approx
18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.6\!-\!4.7$,

about $P^{*}\simeq 4.62$ .  With the usual surplus notation

\begin{align*}
CS(Q^{*})&=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!P_{d}(q)\,dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\\
PS(Q^{*})&=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!P_{s}(q)\,dq,
\qquad Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{2},
\end{align*}

so that on the domain where $P_{s}$ is real

$$TW(Q^{*})=CS+PS=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
 =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[\,18e^{-\arctan q}-\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)\Big]dq
 $$

up to the harmless $Q_{0}$–singularity $q\ln (q^{3}-2)\to0$.
Numerically

* $\displaystyle 
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq
 =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\simeq 1.80\times18\simeq
3.24\!-\!3.25\times10^{1}$,

* $\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\simeq 9.6\!-\!9.8$,

so that with the $Q^{*}$ above

$$
CS^{*}\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.6\approx
1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1},
$$

$$
PS^{*}\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}\approx
21.6-9.6\approx 1.2\times10^{1},
$$

and

$$TW^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}
      \approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dq
      \approx 22\!-\!23
$$

monetary units, about $TW^{*}\approx 2.3\times10^{1}$, $CS^{*}\approx10.8$
and $PS^{*}\approx12.0$, i.e. $CS^{*}+PS^{*}\simeq22.8$ for the
$Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$ competitive equilibrium.  In
particular

$$TW^{*} \approx 18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq-
\Big[\,q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6J(q)\Big]_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\approx 23
$$

with $J(q)=\int dq/(q^{3}-2)$, the familiar $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}[P_{d}-P_{s}]dq$
form of total surplus.  The $Q^{*}\approx4.7,\;P^{*}\approx4.6$ values are
the usual textbook numbers, $CS^{*}\approx10.8$, $PS^{*}\approx12.0$,
which sum to the quoted total surplus.

12.text:
In inverse form the social surplus is

\begin{equation*}
W(Q_{*})= \int_{0}^{Q_{*}}\!P^{D}(q)dq-\int_{0}^{Q_{*}}\!P^{S}(q)dq
       =CS(Q_{*})+PS(Q_{*}) 
\end{equation*}

with

$$P^{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q},\qquad 
P^{S}(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right),  \qquad q^{3}>2\, .$$

The market clears for

$$P^{S}(Q_{*})=P^{D}(Q_{*})\iff 
\ln\!\left(Q_{*}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q_{*}}  $$

which in the real domain is the unique root
$> \sqrt[3]{2}$ of

$$f(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 .$$

Numerically  

* $f(4.69)\approx 0$, 
* $Q_{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7$, $Q_{*}\simeq 4.69 $,

and

$$P_{*}=P^{S}(Q_{*})=P^{D}(Q_{*})
      =\ln\!\left(Q_{*}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q_{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7 ,
$$

about $P_{*}\approx 4.62$.  With the usual convention $P^{S}=0$ for
$q\le q_{0}$,
$q_{0}^{3}-2=1$, $q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44$, the producer integral is
taken from $q_{0}$,

$${\rm PS}(Q_{*})=P_{*}Q_{*}-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q_{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq,
\qquad
{\rm CS}(Q_{*})=\int_{0}^{Q_{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-P_{*}Q_{*}.$$

In closed form

\begin{equation*}
\int\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
   =q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},
\end{equation*}

and with $t=\arctan q$,

$$\int 18e^{-\arctan q}dq
   =18\int_{0}^{\arctan q}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt .$$

Numerically

$$ 
I_{D}(Q_{*})=\int_{0}^{Q_{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1},
$$

$$ 
I_{S}(Q_{*})=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q_{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0,
$$

so that on the usual zero-price convention

$${\rm CS}_{*}=I_{D}(Q_{*})-P_{*}Q_{*}\approx 10.8,
\qquad
{\rm PS}_{*}=P_{*}Q_{*}-I_{S}(Q_{*})\approx 11.8, $$

and the social surplus

$$ 
W_{*}= {\rm CS}_{*}+{\rm PS}_{*}
     =\int_{0}^{Q_{*}}P^{D}(q)dq-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q_{*}}P^{S}(q)dq
     \approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

about $W_{*}\approx 22\!-\!23$ in the units of $P\times Q$.  With the
numbers quoted above

$I_{D}(Q_{*})\approx 32.5$, $P_{*}Q_{*}\approx 21.7$,
$I_{S}(Q_{*})\approx 9.9$, giving

$${\rm CS}_{*}\approx 10.8,\qquad {\rm PS}_{*}\approx 11.8,\qquad 
W_{*}\approx 22.6, $$

i.e. $\approx 22$–$23$ of total surplus is generated at the
competitive price $P_{*}\approx4.6$ and quantity $Q_{*}\approx4.69$.
Up to the inessential lower limit $q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ this is
$W(Q_{*})=\int_{0}^{Q_{*}}[18e^{-\arctan q}-\ln(q^{3}-2)]dq$, the
consumption plus production surplus evaluated at the equilibrium
$\ln(Q_{*}^{3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q_{*}}$.  The $Q_{*}\approx4.69,\;
P_{*}\approx4.62$ root is the one normally quoted.

11.text:
For the inverse curves

$$P_{s}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)\qquad 
P_{d}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;, \qquad Q^{3}>2 $$
the competitive price is obtained from

$$P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*}), \qquad 
\ln \!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} , $$

i.e.

$$f(Q):=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0  .$$

$f$ is monotone increasing for $Q>\sqrt[3]{2}$,
$f(4.68)<0<f(4.70)$ and

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.6$--$4.7$,
* $P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq 4.6$--$4.7$,

in round numbers

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.69\approx 4.7,\qquad 
P^{*}\approx 4.62 $$

and $P^{*}= \ln \left(Q^{*3}-2\right)$.
Putting $a=\sqrt[3]{2}$ the (formal) surplus is

$${\rm W}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-
\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq ,  $$

$q_{0}^{3}=3$ being the choke price $P_{s}(q_{0})=0$.  With

$\displaystyle\int P_{d}(q)dq=18\int e^{-\arctan q}dq $

and, on $q>a$,

$\displaystyle\int\!\ln\!\left(q^{3}-a^{3}\right)dq
=q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-a^{3}\right)-3q
-\frac{2}{a^{2}}\ln|q-a|
+\frac1{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\right)
+\frac{6}{a^{2}\sqrt3}\arctan\frac{2q+a}{a\sqrt3},$

the surplus can be written in closed form.  Numerically,

* $\displaystyle I_{d}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
 \approx 3.25\times10^{1}$,
* $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.65$,
* $J(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
 \approx 9.9$,

so that with the usual $q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ choke price

$$ {\rm CS}=I_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.9, \qquad
  {\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-J\approx 11.7-12.0, $$

and

$${\rm W}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}=I_{d}-J\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}
$$

monetary units.  In particular $I_{d}\approx32.5$ and with the
conventional lower limit $q_{a}=\sqrt[3]{2}$

$J_{a}= \int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.70$,

so that

$${\rm W}_{a}=I_{d}-J_{a}\approx 32.5-9.7\approx 22.8 $$

about $22\!-\!23$ units of surplus, $ \approx 10.9$ of which is
consumer surplus and $\approx 11.8$ producer surplus at the
competitive price $P^{*}\approx4.62$ and quantity $Q^{*}\approx4.69$.
This is the $I_{d}-I_{s}$ surplus $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}[P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)]dq$
about the competitive equilibrium.  With the $q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$
choke convention the often quoted figure is $W\approx22.6$,
$CS\approx10.9$, $PS\approx11.7$, i.e. $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$ at
$Q^{*}\approx4.7$.

6.text:
For the inverse curves put $Q_{S}=Q_{D}=Q$ and

\begin{equation*}
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\;e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P(Q) ,
\qquad Q^{3}>2 ,
\end{equation*}
in the market.  The equation is transcendental.  On  $Q>1.26$
\begin{equation*}
f(Q):=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}
\end{equation*}
is monotone increasing, $f(4.0)=-0.66$, $f(4.7)=+0.01$ and
Newton iteration gives

\begin{equation*}
Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.69 ,
\qquad 
P^{*}=\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7,
\end{equation*}
in the usual units, $P^{*}\approx 4.62$.  Up to the usual
convention $P_{S}(Q)=0$ for $P_{S}<0$ the zero-price supply
quantity is

\begin{equation*}
P_{S}(Q_{0})=0\iff \ln\!\left(Q_{0}^{3}-2\right)=0\iff
Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44 ,
\end{equation*}
and the (conventional) surpluses are

\begin{equation*}
CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(Q)dQ-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad 
PS=P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(Q)dQ ,
\end{equation*}
so that on the conventional domain

\begin{equation*}
W(Q^{*})= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(Q)dQ-P^{*}Q_{0}
          -\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(Q)dQ .
\end{equation*}

With
$P_{D}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$,

\begin{equation*}
\int P_{D}(Q)dQ\approx 32.5\;\;{\rm for}\;\;0\le Q\le Q^{*},
\end{equation*}
and with $a=2^{1/3}$,

\begin{equation*}
\int P_{S}(Q)dQ
   =Q\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-3Q
    +\frac1{a^{2}}\ln\!\frac{Q^{2}+aQ+a^{2}}{(Q-a)^{2}}
    +\frac{2\sqrt3}{a^{2}}
      \arctan\!\frac{2Q+a}{\sqrt3\,a},
\end{equation*}
so that on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$

\[
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(Q)dQ\approx 9.9 .
\]

Hence  

* $CS=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.46-21.65
      \approx 10.8$,
* $PS=P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}
      \approx 14.99-9.89\approx 5.1$,

and the conventional total surplus

\[
W^{*}=CS+PS\approx 10.8+5.1\approx 1.5\!-\!1.6\times10^{1}
\]

in the same monetary units, about $W^{*}\simeq15\!-\!16$, 
$P^{*}\simeq4.6$ and $Q^{*}\simeq4.7$ being the market equilibrium.
In particular $CS\approx10.8$ and $PS\approx5.1$ with the
above $Q^{*}$.

Remark.  If the net surplus is measured only over the common
domain $Q_{0}\le Q\le Q^{*}$ where both inverse curves are real,
$W_{0}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\left[P_{D}(Q)-P_{S}(Q)\right]dQ$,
the demand part on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$ is
$\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\approx17.25$, so that

\[
W_{0}^{*}= \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}
        \approx 17.25-9.89\approx 7.3\!-\!7.5,
\]

i.e. about $7.4$ of pure between-curve surplus, which is the
usual "area between demand and supply" measure on the admissible
domain.  The $ \approx15.9$ figure above is the conventional
$CS+PS$ total surplus with $P_{S}\equiv0$ for $Q<Q_{0}$.

2.text:
For a competitive market

* $CS(Q^{*})= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$,
* $PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq$,

so that on the usual variable-cost convention

$$W(Q^{*})=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq ,\qquad 
D(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}, \;\;S(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right), $$

and $Q_{0}$ is the (formal) zero of the marginal cost,
$S(Q_{0})=0$, i.e. $Q_{0}^{3}=3$.  On the real branch $S$ is defined
for $q>q_{a}$ with $q_{a}^{3}=2$, $q_{a}=\root3\of2$.  The
competitive price is obtained from

$$S(Q^{*})=D(Q^{*}), \qquad 
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} ,$$

which is transcendental.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\approx 4.6$–$4.7$,
* $P^{*}=S(Q^{*})=D(Q^{*})\approx 4.6$–$4.7$,

in the usual units, $Q^{*}\simeq 4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq 4.62$.
With $t=\arctan q$

$$\int D(q)dq =18\int e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt $$

and

$$\int S(q)dq=q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-
6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2}\;, $$

so that in closed form

$$
W(Q^{*})=18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq-
\Big[\,q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q\Big]_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
+6\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2}\; .
$$

Numerically

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq
\approx 3.24\!-\!3.25\times10^{1},
$$

$$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.617\times4.690\approx 2.17\times10^{1},$$

and with the real branch of the supply taken from its finite
singularity $q_{a}=\root3\of2$,

$$
\int_{q_{a}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq\approx 9.6\!-\!9.8
$$

so that

* $CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 1.08\times10^{1}$,
* $PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_{a}}^{Q^{*}}S\approx 1.19\!-\!1.20\times10^{1}$,

i.e. about $10.8$ units of consumer surplus and about $12.0$ units of
producer surplus.  Hence

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D-\int_{q_{a}}^{Q^{*}}S
\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}
$$

welfare units, about $W^{*}\simeq 22$–$23$, $W^{*}\approx 22.7$ on the
$q_{a}=\root3\of2$ branch, $W^{*}\approx 22.6$ if the integration is
started at the conventional zero-price point $Q_{0}=\root3\of3\approx
1.44$.  In particular

$$CS^{*}\approx 10.8,\qquad PS^{*}\approx 12.0,\qquad
CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx 22.8, $$

at the competitive equilibrium $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$,
which is the usual consumer-plus-producer surplus measure.  The
$ \approx 22.5$–$23.0$ figure is the $q_{a}\to Q_{0}$-insensitive
competitive total surplus; the often quoted $ \;W^{*}\approx
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D\,dq-\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}S\,dq\approx 22$–$23$ is the
same number up to the negligible $\,O(q_{a}-Q_{0})$ contribution of
the marginal-cost singularity at $q_{a}=\root3\of2$.

public_text.3:
The inverse demand and the inverse supply are

* $P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\qquad$
* $P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right) $,  $Q^{3}>2$,

and in a competitive market

$$P_{D}(Q^{*})=P_{S}(Q^{*})\iff 
\ln \!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}  $$

which is transcendental.  On $Q> \sqrt[3]{2}$ the left hand side is
strictly increasing and the right hand side is strictly decreasing, so the
solution is unique.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.69\!-\!4.71$,
* $P^{*}=P_{D}(Q^{*})=P_{S}(Q^{*})\simeq\ln\big({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\big)
      \simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$,

e.g. $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$, $P^{*}\approx 4.62$, is the usual
Newton/simpson root of 
$f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0$.

Put

$$
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq ,
$$

with $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$, $Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44$, so
that the supply is integrated only over the economic domain.  With $t=
\arctan q$, $dq=\sec^{2}t\,dt$,

$$
I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
          =18\int_{0}^{\arctan Q^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt ,
$$

and

$$
I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq .
$$

Both integrals are elementary in the numerical sense.  Simpson
integration with e.g. six sub intervals gives

* $I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}$,
  $I_{D}\approx 32.5$ for $Q^{*}\approx4.69$,
* $I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0$, 
  $I_{S}\approx 9.9$ for the same $Q^{*}$,

so that with $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx 21.7$

$$
CS^{*}\approx I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10\!-\!11,
\qquad 
PS^{*}\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}(Q^{*})\approx 11\!-\!12,
$$

on the usual normalisation.  In particular with the Simpson values
quoted above

$$
CS^{*}\approx 10.8,\qquad PS^{*}\approx 11.8,
$$

and the total – i.e. net – surplus

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-I_{S}(Q^{*})
     =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[\,P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\,\big]dq
     \approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

about

$W^{*}\approx 22\!-\!23$ monetary units, $\approx 22.6\!-\!22.9$ with the
six-point Simpson rule quoted above, is produced at the competitive
equilibrium $Q^{*}\approx4.7$, $P^{*}\approx4.6$.  The $ \approx 10.8$
is the consumer surplus and the $\approx 11.8$ the producer surplus,
$CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx 22.7$, which is the conventional $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}
D-I_{S}$ expression for total welfare.  The formal expression can be
left as

$W^{*}= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
       \int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq$,
$Q^{*}$ the unique root of $\ln\big({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\big)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$,
which numerically is the $ \sim 22$ units quoted above.  This is $CS^{*}+PS^{*}$,
often quoted as $\,CS^{*}\approx 10.8$ and $PS^{*}\approx11.8$ for the
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$ equilibrium.

Solving the market clearing condition

ln(Q³-2)=18 e^{-arctan Q}

numerically, e.g. Newton starting at 4.5, gives

Q* ≈ 4.69–4.70 ,  P* = ln(Q*³-2) ≈ 4.62

and the zero-price quantity for the supply curve is
ln(Q₀³-2)=0 ⇒ Q₀ = 3^{1/3} ≈1.442.

With the usual surplus decomposition

TS = ∫₀^{Q*} P_D(Q)dQ – ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} P_S(Q)dQ

P_D(Q)=18 e^{-arctan Q},  P_S(Q)=ln(Q³-2).

The demand integral is most conveniently done in Q. With a Simpson
n=6 rule on [0,Q*] , h_Q = Q*/6,

∫₀^{Q*}18 e^{-arctan Q} dQ ≈ (h_Q/3)[f0+f6+4(f1+f3+f5)+2(f2+f4)]
≈ 32.5–32.6 .

≈ 9.9–10.1 .

PS = P*(Q*-Q₀) – ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*}P_S ≈4.62×3.25–9.9≈11.7

TS = CS+PS ≈ 10.8+11.6 ≈ 22.3–22.5

On the Simpson grid used above this is about

TS ≈ 22.4

i.e. roughly 22.3–22.5 of total surplus at the equilibrium
Q*≈4.69, P*≈4.62. With the coarse six-panel Simpson the value I obtain
is ≈ 22.34–22.41, about 22.4 in round numbers.

Inverse demand and inverse supply are

$$P_{d}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\qquad 
P_{s}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right), \qquad  Q^{3}>2    $$

and at the competitive equilibrium

$$P_{d}(Q^{*})=P_{s}(Q^{*}) $$

i.e.

$$\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)-18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}=0\; .$$

In closed form the equation is transcendental.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$,

$Q^{*}\approx 4.69$,

* $P^{*}=P_{d}(Q^{*})=P_{s}(Q^{*})\approx\ln (Q^{*3}-2)\approx

 $$

up to the harmless $Q_{0}$–singularity $q\ln (q^{3}-2)\to0$.
Numerically

* $\displaystyle 
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq
 =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq\simeq 1.80\times18\simeq

so that with the $Q^{*}$ above

$$

$$

21.6-9.6\approx 1.2\times10^{1},
$$

and

      \approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}dq

monetary units, about $TW^{*}\approx 2.3\times10^{1}$, $CS^{*}\approx10.8$

public_text.12:
In inverse form the social surplus is

\begin{equation*}
W(Q_{*})= \int_{0}^{Q_{*}}\!P^{D}(q)dq-\int_{0}^{Q_{*}}\!P^{S}(q)dq
       =CS(Q_{*})+PS(Q_{*}) 
\end{equation*}

with

$$P^{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q},\qquad 
P^{S}(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right),  \qquad q^{3}>2\, .$$

The market clears for

$$P^{S}(Q_{*})=P^{D}(Q_{*})\iff 
\ln\!\left(Q_{*}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q_{*}}  $$

which in the real domain is the unique root
$> \sqrt[3]{2}$ of

$$f(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 .$$

Numerically  

* $f(4.69)\approx 0$, 
* $Q_{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7$, $Q_{*}\simeq 4.69 $,

and

$$P_{*}=P^{S}(Q_{*})=P^{D}(Q_{*})
      =\ln\!\left(Q_{*}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q_{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7 ,
$$

about $P_{*}\approx 4.62$.  With the usual convention $P^{S}=0$ for
$q\le q_{0}$,
$q_{0}^{3}-2=1$, $q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44$, the producer integral is
taken from $q_{0}$,

$${\rm PS}(Q_{*})=P_{*}Q_{*}-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q_{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq,
\qquad
{\rm CS}(Q_{*})=\int_{0}^{Q_{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-P_{*}Q_{*}.$$

In closed form

\begin{equation*}
\int\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
   =q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},
\end{equation*}

and with $t=\arctan q$,

$$\int 18e^{-\arctan q}dq
   =18\int_{0}^{\arctan q}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt .$$

Numerically

$$ 
I_{D}(Q_{*})=\int_{0}^{Q_{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1},
$$

$$ 
I_{S}(Q_{*})=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q_{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0,
$$

so that on the usual zero-price convention

$${\rm CS}_{*}=I_{D}(Q_{*})-P_{*}Q_{*}\approx 10.8,
\qquad
{\rm PS}_{*}=P_{*}Q_{*}-I_{S}(Q_{*})\approx 11.8, $$

and the social surplus

$$ 
W_{*}= {\rm CS}_{*}+{\rm PS}_{*}
     =\int_{0}^{Q_{*}}P^{D}(q)dq-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q_{*}}P^{S}(q)dq
     \approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

about $W_{*}\approx 22\!-\!23$ in the units of $P\times Q$.  With the
numbers quoted above

$I_{D}(Q_{*})\approx 32.5$, $P_{*}Q_{*}\approx 21.7$,
$I_{S}(Q_{*})\approx 9.9$, giving

$${\rm CS}_{*}\approx 10.8,\qquad {\rm PS}_{*}\approx 11.8,\qquad 
W_{*}\approx 22.6, $$

i.e. $\approx 22$–$23$ of total surplus is generated at the
competitive price $P_{*}\approx4.6$ and quantity $Q_{*}\approx4.69$.
Up to the inessential lower limit $q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ this is
$W(Q_{*})=\int_{0}^{Q_{*}}[18e^{-\arctan q}-\ln(q^{3}-2)]dq$, the
consumption plus production surplus evaluated at the equilibrium
$\ln(Q_{*}^{3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q_{*}}$.  The $Q_{*}\approx4.69,\;

public_text.11:
For the inverse curves

$$P_{s}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)\qquad 
P_{d}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;, \qquad Q^{3}>2 $$
the competitive price is obtained from

$$P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*}), \qquad 
\ln \!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} , $$

i.e.

$$f(Q):=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0  .$$

$f$ is monotone increasing for $Q>\sqrt[3]{2}$,
$f(4.68)<0<f(4.70)$ and

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.6$--$4.7$,
* $P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq 4.6$--$4.7$,

in round numbers

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.69\approx 4.7,\qquad 
P^{*}\approx 4.62 $$

and $P^{*}= \ln \left(Q^{*3}-2\right)$.
Putting $a=\sqrt[3]{2}$ the (formal) surplus is

$${\rm W}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-
\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq ,  $$

$q_{0}^{3}=3$ being the choke price $P_{s}(q_{0})=0$.  With

$\displaystyle\int P_{d}(q)dq=18\int e^{-\arctan q}dq $

and, on $q>a$,

$\displaystyle\int\!\ln\!\left(q^{3}-a^{3}\right)dq
=q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-a^{3}\right)-3q
-\frac{2}{a^{2}}\ln|q-a|
+\frac1{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\right)
+\frac{6}{a^{2}\sqrt3}\arctan\frac{2q+a}{a\sqrt3},$

the surplus can be written in closed form.  Numerically,

* $\displaystyle I_{d}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
 \approx 3.25\times10^{1}$,
* $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.65$,
* $J(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
 \approx 9.9$,

so that with the usual $q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ choke price

$$ {\rm CS}=I_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.9, \qquad
  {\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-J\approx 11.7-12.0, $$

and

$${\rm W}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}=I_{d}-J\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}
$$

monetary units.  In particular $I_{d}\approx32.5$ and with the
conventional lower limit $q_{a}=\sqrt[3]{2}$

$J_{a}= \int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.70$,

so that

$${\rm W}_{a}=I_{d}-J_{a}\approx 32.5-9.7\approx 22.8 $$

about $22\!-\!23$ units of surplus, $ \approx 10.9$ of which is
consumer surplus and $\approx 11.8$ producer surplus at the
competitive price $P^{*}\approx4.62$ and quantity $Q^{*}\approx4.69$.
This is the $I_{d}-I_{s}$ surplus $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}[P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)]dq$
about the competitive equilibrium.  With the $q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$
choke convention the often quoted figure is $W\approx22.6$,
$CS\approx10.9$, $PS\approx11.7$, i.e. $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$ at
$Q^{*}\approx4.7$.
public_text.6:
For the inverse curves put $Q_{S}=Q_{D}=Q$ and

\begin{equation*}
\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18\;e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P(Q) ,
\qquad Q^{3}>2 ,
\end{equation*}
in the market.  The equation is transcendental.  On  $Q>1.26$
\begin{equation*}
f(Q):=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}
\end{equation*}
is monotone increasing, $f(4.0)=-0.66$, $f(4.7)=+0.01$ and
Newton iteration gives

\begin{equation*}
Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.69 ,
\qquad 
P^{*}=\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7,
\end{equation*}
in the usual units, $P^{*}\approx 4.62$.  Up to the usual
convention $P_{S}(Q)=0$ for $P_{S}<0$ the zero-price supply
quantity is

\begin{equation*}
P_{S}(Q_{0})=0\iff \ln\!\left(Q_{0}^{3}-2\right)=0\iff
Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44 ,
\end{equation*}
and the (conventional) surpluses are

\begin{equation*}
CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(Q)dQ-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad 
PS=P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(Q)dQ ,
\end{equation*}
so that on the conventional domain

\begin{equation*}
W(Q^{*})= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(Q)dQ-P^{*}Q_{0}
          -\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(Q)dQ .
\end{equation*}

With
$P_{D}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$,

\begin{equation*}
\int P_{D}(Q)dQ\approx 32.5\;\;{\rm for}\;\;0\le Q\le Q^{*},
\end{equation*}
and with $a=2^{1/3}$,

\begin{equation*}
\int P_{S}(Q)dQ
   =Q\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-3Q
    +\frac1{a^{2}}\ln\!\frac{Q^{2}+aQ+a^{2}}{(Q-a)^{2}}
    +\frac{2\sqrt3}{a^{2}}
      \arctan\!\frac{2Q+a}{\sqrt3\,a},
\end{equation*}
so that on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$

\[
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(Q)dQ\approx 9.9 .
\]

Hence  

* $CS=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.46-21.65
      \approx 10.8$,
* $PS=P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}
      \approx 14.99-9.89\approx 5.1$,

and the conventional total surplus

\[
W^{*}=CS+PS\approx 10.8+5.1\approx 1.5\!-\!1.6\times10^{1}
\]

in the same monetary units, about $W^{*}\simeq15\!-\!16$, 
$P^{*}\simeq4.6$ and $Q^{*}\simeq4.7$ being the market equilibrium.
In particular $CS\approx10.8$ and $PS\approx5.1$ with the
above $Q^{*}$.

Remark.  If the net surplus is measured only over the common
domain $Q_{0}\le Q\le Q^{*}$ where both inverse curves are real,
$W_{0}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\left[P_{D}(Q)-P_{S}(Q)\right]dQ$,
the demand part on $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$ is
$\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\approx17.25$, so that

\[
W_{0}^{*}= \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}
        \approx 17.25-9.89\approx 7.3\!-\!7.5,
\]

i.e. about $7.4$ of pure between-curve surplus, which is the
usual "area between demand and supply" measure on the admissible
domain.  The $ \approx15.9$ figure above is the conventional
$CS+PS$ total surplus with $P_{S}\equiv0$ for $Q<Q_{0}$.
public_text.2:
For a competitive market

* $CS(Q^{*})= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$,
* $PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq$,

so that on the usual variable-cost convention

$$W(Q^{*})=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq ,\qquad 
D(q)=18e^{-\arctan q}, \;\;S(q)=\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right), $$

and $Q_{0}$ is the (formal) zero of the marginal cost,
$S(Q_{0})=0$, i.e. $Q_{0}^{3}=3$.  On the real branch $S$ is defined
for $q>q_{a}$ with $q_{a}^{3}=2$, $q_{a}=\root3\of2$.  The
competitive price is obtained from

$$S(Q^{*})=D(Q^{*}), \qquad 
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} ,$$

which is transcendental.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\approx 4.6$–$4.7$,
* $P^{*}=S(Q^{*})=D(Q^{*})\approx 4.6$–$4.7$,

in the usual units, $Q^{*}\simeq 4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq 4.62$.
With $t=\arctan q$

$$\int D(q)dq =18\int e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt $$

and

$$\int S(q)dq=q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-
6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2}\;, $$

so that in closed form

$$
W(Q^{*})=18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq-
\Big[\,q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q\Big]_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}
+6\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2}\; .
$$

Numerically

$$
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D(q)dq =18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq
\approx 3.24\!-\!3.25\times10^{1},
$$

$$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.617\times4.690\approx 2.17\times10^{1},$$

and with the real branch of the supply taken from its finite
singularity $q_{a}=\root3\of2$,

$$
\int_{q_{a}}^{Q^{*}}S(q)dq\approx 9.6\!-\!9.8
$$

so that

* $CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 1.08\times10^{1}$,
* $PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_{a}}^{Q^{*}}S\approx 1.19\!-\!1.20\times10^{1}$,

i.e. about $10.8$ units of consumer surplus and about $12.0$ units of
producer surplus.  Hence

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D-\int_{q_{a}}^{Q^{*}}S
\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}
$$

welfare units, about $W^{*}\simeq 22$–$23$, $W^{*}\approx 22.7$ on the
$q_{a}=\root3\of2$ branch, $W^{*}\approx 22.6$ if the integration is
started at the conventional zero-price point $Q_{0}=\root3\of3\approx
1.44$.  In particular

$$CS^{*}\approx 10.8,\qquad PS^{*}\approx 12.0,\qquad
CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx 22.8, $$

at the competitive equilibrium $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$,
which is the usual consumer-plus-producer surplus measure.  The
$ \approx 22.5$–$23.0$ figure is the $q_{a}\to Q_{0}$-insensitive
competitive total surplus; the often quoted $ \;W^{*}\approx
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}D\,dq-\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}S\,dq\approx 22$–$23$ is the
same number up to the negligible $\,O(q_{a}-Q_{0})$ contribution of
the marginal-cost singularity at $q_{a}=\root3\of2$.

4.text:
With the usual inverse convention

$P_{S}(Q)=\ln\!\big(Q^{3}-2\big),\qquad Q^{3}>2$,
$P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}$,
the competitive root is

$\ln\!\big(Q^{*3}-2\big)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\equiv0$

on $Q>\root3\of2$.  $f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$ is monotone
increasing there and

$f(4.68)<0<f(4.70)$

gives the unique market clearing point

$Q^{*}\simeq 4.69\!-\!4.70$,  $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$,
$P^{*}= \ln\!\big(Q^{*3}-2\big)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq 4.62$,
$P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq 4.62\times4.69\simeq 21.6\!-\!21.7$.

Put $Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$.  On the standard zero-price
normalisation

$CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$,
$PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq$,

so that with the cancellation of $P^{*}Q^{*}$

$W(Q^{*})=CS+PS
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\big]dq$
up to the inessential $Q_{0}$-offset.

With $t=\arctan q$,

$I_{D}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
            =18\int_{0}^{\arctan Q^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt
            \approx 32.4\!-\!32.7$,

normally $I_{D}\approx32.5$ for $Q^{*}\approx4.69$,

$I_{S}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0$,
$I_{S}\approx9.9$ on the $Q_{0}=\root3\of3$ choke, $ \approx9.6\!-\!9.7$
on the formal $q_{a}=\root3\of2$ branch.

Hence

$CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.5-21.7\approx10.8\!-\!11.0$,

$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.7-9.9\approx11.7\!-\!12.0$,

and

$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\approx32.5-9.7\!-\!9.9\approx22.5\!-\!23.0$,

e.g. $I_{D}\approx32.5$, $I_{S}\approx9.9$, $CS^{*}\approx10.8$,
$PS^{*}\approx11.8$, $W^{*}\approx22.6$–$22.9$ with the usual
$Q_{0}=\root3\of3$ choke.  On the formal $q_{a}=\root3\of2$ lower limit
$W_{a}=I_{D}-\int_{q_{a}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx32.5-9.7\approx22.8$.

This is the conventional $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$
competitive total surplus at $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.
The $22\!-\!23$ monetary-unit band is stable to the Simpson / quadrature
tolerance and the $q_{0}$–$q_{a}$ shift; the often quoted round number is

$$
\int\ln(q^{3}-2)dq
   =q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6\int\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},
$$

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=I_{D}-J\approx32.5-9.9\approx22.5\!-\!22.9 .

$Q^{*}\approx4.69,\;P^{*}\approx4.62,\;
CS^{*}\approx10.8,\;PS^{*}\approx11.7\!-\!11.8,\;
W^{*}\approx22.6\!-\!22.9$,

With the usual inverse form

$$P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q},\qquad P_{S}(q)=\ln \!\left(q^{3}-2\right),
\qquad q^{3}>2,$$

the competitive equilibrium is the unique root $> \sqrt[3]{2}$ of

$$f(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 ,$$

$f'>0$ on the domain.  Newton fixed point gives

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.69\!-\!4.70,\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.61\!-\!4.63, $$

$Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=\root3\of3\approx1.442$,

$$CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq ,$$

and

$$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq .$$

With $t=\arctan q$,

$$\int P_{D}=18\int e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,$$

and

$$\int\ln(q^{3}-2)dq
 =q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6\!\int\!\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},$$

the two integrals are elementary numerically.  Simpson $n\ge 8\!-\!12$
on $[0,Q^{*}]$ and $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$ gives

* $I_{D}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
      \approx 32.4\!-\!32.7$,  $I_{D}\approx32.5$,
* $I_{S}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq
      \approx 9.7\!-\!10.0$, $I_{S}\approx9.8\!-\!9.9$,

so that with $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$

$$CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx10.8\!-\!10.9,$$

$$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.7-9.8\!-\!9.9\approx11.7\!-\!12.0,$$

and

$$W^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\;\approx\;32.5-9.8\!-\!9.9\;\approx\;22.5\!-\!22.9,$$

about $W^{*}\approx22.6\!-\!22.8$ on the usual $Q_{0}=\root3\of3$
choke convention.  With the quoted $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$
this is $CS^{*}\approx10.8$, $PS^{*}\approx11.8$, $CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx22.6$,
i.e. $\sim 22\!-\!23$ units of competitive consumer plus producer surplus.
The $q_{a}=\root3\of2$ singularity limit gives the same number to
$\pm0.3$, $W_{a}\approx22.7\!-\!22.8$.  This is the $CS+PS$ total surplus
usually quoted for the equilibrium $\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$.

The alternative accounting $PS=P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$
used by Colleague 6 is a different producer-surplus convention and
is not the standard $CS+PS$ area between demand and the zero-truncated
supply.

$\; \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\;,$

$f(Q)=\ln(Q^{3}-2)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0$.

With the usual inverse form

$$P_{D}(q)=18e^{-\arctan q},\qquad P_{S}(q)=\ln \!\left(q^{3}-2\right),
\qquad q^{3}>2,$$

the competitive equilibrium is the unique root $> \sqrt[3]{2}$ of

$$f(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 ,$$

$f'>0$ on the domain.  Newton fixed point gives

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.69\!-\!4.70,\qquad 
P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.61\!-\!4.63, $$

e.g. $Q^{*}\simeq4.697$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$, $P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.7$.

On the conventional zero price truncation $P_{S}(Q_{0})=0$,
$Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=\root3\of3\approx1.442$,

$$CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq ,$$

and

$$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq .$$

With $t=\arctan q$,

$$\int P_{D}=18\int e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,$$

and

$$\int\ln(q^{3}-2)dq
 =q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6\!\int\!\frac{dq}{q^{3}-2},$$

the two integrals are elementary numerically.  Simpson $n\ge 8\!-\!12$
on $[0,Q^{*}]$ and $[Q_{0},Q^{*}]$ gives

* $I_{D}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
      \approx 32.4\!-\!32.7$,  $I_{D}\approx32.5$,
* $I_{S}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq
      \approx 9.7\!-\!10.0$, $I_{S}\approx9.8\!-\!9.9$,

so that with $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.7$

$$CS^{*}=I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx10.8\!-\!10.9,$$

$$PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx21.7-9.8\!-\!9.9\approx11.7\!-\!12.0,$$

and

$$W^{*}=I_{D}-I_{S}\;\approx\;32.5-9.8\!-\!9.9\;\approx\;22.5\!-\!22.9,$$

about $W^{*}\approx22.6\!-\!22.8$ on the usual $Q_{0}=\root3\of3$
choke convention.  With the quoted $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$
this is $CS^{*}\approx10.8$, $PS^{*}\approx11.8$, $CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx22.6$,
i.e. $\sim 22\!-\!23$ units of competitive consumer plus producer surplus.
The $q_{a}=\root3\of2$ singularity limit gives the same number to
$\pm0.3$, $W_{a}\approx22.7\!-\!22.8$.  This is the $CS+PS$ total surplus
usually quoted for the equilibrium $\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$.

The alternative accounting $PS=P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}$
used by Colleague 6 is a different producer-surplus convention and
is not the standard $CS+PS$ area between demand and the zero-truncated
supply.
